common_name: Abate Fetel Pear (Elongated Italian Dessert Pear)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer; Abate Fetel is a late-season variety that stores exceptionally well in cold storage.

directions: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer. Bred beginning in 1865 by the French abbot Fetel, first at Chessy in the Rhône and later at Charentay, it is instantly recognizable by its long, slender, bottle-like shape and pale green-yellow, lightly russeted skin, with white, fine-grained, very sweet and juicy flesh. It has become the most widely produced and exported pear cultivar in Italy, concentrated in the Emilia-Romagna region under Protected Geographical Indication status, prized for both its elegant form and its long storage life of up to several months under refrigeration. Harvest in September while still firm, then hold in cold storage and ripen at room temperature for a few days before eating.

common_name: Coscia Pear (Ercolini, Ancient Italian Summer Pear)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Coscia is an early-ripening summer pear best picked and eaten promptly since it softens quickly.

directions: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. An ancient Italian landrace also known as Ercolini, it bears small, elongated fruit with green skin that turns yellow as it ripens, with white, juicy, sweet flesh carrying a faint spicy note, ripening in late summer ahead of most other European dessert pears. The tree is vigorous and highly productive, especially in the warmer growing regions of central and southern Italy, and while partially self-fertile it sets a heavier crop with a second pear variety nearby for cross-pollination. Harvest as soon as the skin begins to yellow and eat promptly, since the fruit ripens and softens quickly off the tree.
sources: PMC — Characterization and Phylogenetic Analysis of Ancient Italian Landraces of Pear

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with two compatible pollinizers, since Beurre Diel is a self-sterile triploid; it needs a warm site and a good summer to ripen well.

directions: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with two compatible pollinizers. Found around 1800 as a wilding near Vilvoorde, Belgium by Meuris, head gardener to the famed pomologist Van Mons, and named for the German pomologist Diel, it bears medium to large, round-to-oval fruit with dull yellowish-green, slightly rough skin marked with russet patches, and creamy white, juicy, melting flesh with an excellent sweet flavor when properly ripened. Because it is a triploid it cannot pollinate other pears and requires two other varieties planted nearby. Harvest in fall while still firm, then ripen at room temperature for a week or more until the flesh yields to gentle pressure.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in a warm, sheltered site, ideally against a wall or fence; Josephine de Malines is not very vigorous and bruises easily, so handle the ripe fruit gently.

directions: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in a warm, sheltered site. Raised by Major Esperen at Malines, Belgium in 1830 and named for his wife, it bears heavy crops of small, conical, greenish-yellow fruit with a dark red flush, and smooth, melting, white flesh with a sweet, fine, aromatic flavor that earned it a Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit. A late winter pear usable from November into December or January, it shows good resistance to pear scab and keeps well into the new year, though its lack of vigor and delicate skin reward a sheltered planting site and careful handling. Harvest in mid-to-late fall while still firm, store cool for several weeks, then finish ripening at room temperature before eating.

common_name: Catillac Pear (Historic French Culinary and Perry Pear)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with two compatible pollinizers, since Catillac is a triploid; the hard fruit is grown for slow cooking rather than fresh eating.

directions: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with two compatible pollinizers. A historic French pear grown in the gardens of Louis XIV at Versailles and first described in 1665, it bears large, hard fruit with slightly gritty flesh that turns an attractive pink when cooked, and greenish-yellow skin with a dull red blush at maturity. Suitable only for very slow cooking rather than fresh eating, it is a long-established culinary pear of high quality that can also be pressed for perry, and the vigorous, reliable, hardy tree produces fruit that keeps exceptionally well after a mid-autumn harvest. Harvest in mid-autumn once firm and mature, store cool, and cook slowly whole or in pieces until the flesh turns pink and tender.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil, tolerant of cooler and shadier sites than most pears; Jargonelle is a triploid and needs two other pear varieties nearby for pollination.

directions: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil, tolerant of cooler and shadier sites than most pears. One of the oldest pears still in cultivation, dating to at least the early 1600s and first recorded by John Parkinson in 1629, it likely originated in Anjou, France. The long, small, calabash-shaped fruit has tender, melting, juicy flesh with a distinctive musky flavor, ripening very early in August ahead of nearly all other European pears. The tree is notably hardy and long-lived, tolerating walls and cooler northern sites without full sun better than most pear varieties. Harvest in early August as the fruit softens, and eat promptly since it does not keep.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer; Glou Morceau is a late-season winter pear that keeps well after harvest.

directions: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer. Raised around 1750 by the Abbé Hardenpont of Mons, Belgium and also known as Beurré d'Hardenpont, it was introduced to Britain in 1820 and became immensely popular in Victorian England before nearly disappearing from modern markets. The medium-to-large, pyriform fruit has semi-smooth, pale olive-green skin covered in brown russet patches and specks, with ivory to off-white flesh that is moist, soft, fine-grained, and melting, sweet with a delicate sugary flavor; its name translates as "delicious morsel." Harvest in fall while still firm, store cool for several weeks, then ripen at room temperature until the buttery flesh softens before eating.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer; Easter Beurre is an extremely late-ripening winter pear that needs weeks of cold storage before eating.

directions: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer. Originating around 1823 at the Capucin Monastery at Louvain, Belgium, where monks knew it as Pastorale de Louvain, it is also known in France as Doyenné d'Hiver. The obovate-pyriform fruit has yellow skin marked with conspicuous russet dots and patches, often with a dull brownish-red blush, and yellow-tinged, tender, melting, buttery flesh with a rich, aromatic, sweet flavor. The tree is medium-sized, vigorous, upright-spreading, and slow-growing; historically its very long keeping quality made it valuable for extending the fresh pear season into late winter and spring. Harvest quite late in fall while very hard, store cool for many weeks, then finish ripening at room temperature before eating.
sources: Chest of Books — historical pomology reference

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with two compatible pollinizers, since Merton Pride is a triploid and will not pollinate other pear trees.

directions: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with two compatible pollinizers. Raised in 1941 by M.B. Crane at the John Innes Horticultural Institute in Merton, London, from a cross of Glou Morceau and Double Williams, it was renamed Merton Pride in 1957 after initially being called Merton Favourite. The large, conical to pyriform fruit has rough green skin ripening to yellow with variable brown russet, and creamy white, soft, smooth, very juicy flesh with excellent sweet, melting texture and good pear flavor. The tree is a moderate cropper with some biennial tendency, ripening its fruit in September. Harvest in September while firm, then ripen at room temperature for several days before eating.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Gorham is self-fertile and also an excellent pollinizer for other European pear varieties planted nearby.

directions: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Raised in 1910 by Richard Wellington at the New York State Agricultural Experiment Station in Geneva from a cross of Williams Bon Chrétien (Bartlett) and Josephine de Malines, it was introduced to Britain in 1923 and received a Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit. The small-to-medium fruit has pale green skin turning pale yellow, sometimes entirely covered in light brown russet, with fine, juicy, cream-colored flesh carrying a sweet, musky flavor reminiscent of its Bartlett parent. It shows high resistance to scab and good resistance to mildew, making it a reliable, low-fuss choice for a home orchard. Harvest in early-to-mid fall while firm, then ripen at room temperature for several days before eating.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Honeysweet is self-fertile, one of the few pears that reliably sets fruit without a separate pollinizer.

directions: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Selected from 137 seedlings screened for fire blight survival and winter hardiness at Purdue University and released by the USDA, it combines a comparatively high level of fire blight resistance, similar to Kieffer and notably better than Seckel, with genuinely sweet, dessert-quality flavor rather than the tough, mediocre-eating fruit typical of many blight-resistant pears. The medium-sized, classically pear-shaped fruit has yellow skin with russet freckling at maturity and white, fine-grained, very juicy, smooth flesh. Harvest in fall while firm, then ripen at room temperature for several days before eating.
sources: SHAP — New Fire Blight Resistant Pear Cultivars

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer such as Bartlett; Starkrimson ripens early and softens quickly, so pick and handle it promptly.

directions: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer such as Bartlett. Discovered as a brilliant crimson-red bud sport of Clapp's Favorite by Adrian G. Kalle of South Haven, Michigan, and introduced under the trademarked name Starkrimson by Stark Bro's Nursery in 1970, it is also known informally as Red Clapp's. The fruit has striking, glossy red skin with a thick, stocky stem and dense white flesh, offering a mild, sweet flavor with a subtle floral aroma and smooth, juicy texture. As an early summer pear it is typically among the first fresh pears of the season, ready from August. Harvest while still firm and deeply colored in late summer, then ripen at room temperature for a few days and eat promptly.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Improved Fertility is partially self-fertile and one of the most heavily cropping English pear varieties.

directions: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. An improved sport selected from the older English variety Fertility, it retains its parent's hardiness and remarkably heavy, reliable cropping while offering somewhat better dessert quality, bearing medium-sized fruit that is very sweet and juicy with a melting texture. Its partial self-fertility makes it a forgiving choice for a small home orchard with room for only one or two pear trees, though cropping still improves with a second variety nearby. Harvest in early-to-mid fall while firm, then ripen at room temperature for a few days before eating.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in a warm, sheltered site with a compatible pollinizer; Beurre Superfin needs good summer heat to fully develop its flavor.

directions: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in a warm, sheltered site with a compatible pollinizer. Raised near Angers, France in 1837, it ripens in late September, bearing round-conical fruit that turns from green to yellow with light brown russet as it matures, with creamy yellow, melting flesh considered among the finest-flavored of the classic French dessert pears. A high-quality variety, it rewards a warm, sheltered planting site with excellent buttery, aromatic fruit, though it performs poorly in cool or exposed locations. Harvest in late September while firm, then ripen at room temperature for several days before eating.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer, since Nouveau Poiteau is self-sterile.

directions: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer. An old French and Belgian heirloom pear named for the French botanist and pomologist Antoine Poiteau, it is valued above all as a reliable, heavy-cropping variety, with good if not outstanding dessert flavor and texture. Its consistent, generous yields made it a long-standing orchard staple in Europe even though showier or better-flavored varieties were available. Harvest in fall while firm, then ripen at room temperature for a few days before eating.

common_name: Black Worcester Pear (Historic English Culinary Pear)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer; Black Worcester is grown for cooking rather than fresh eating and keeps very well in storage.

directions: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer. One of England's oldest named pear cultivars, dating back for centuries and long associated with the city of Worcester, whose coat of arms depicts three of its distinctive dark fruits, it bears hard, dense pears covered in a dull, purplish, near-black skin that sets it apart from nearly every other pear variety. The dense, gritty flesh is unsuitable for fresh eating but excellent baked, poached, or stewed, and the fruit keeps exceptionally well in storage over winter. Harvest in mid-autumn once mature, store cool, and cook whole or sliced until the flesh softens and turns tender.

planting.note: Plant dormant, grafted trees in early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Yellow Huffcap fruit must be gathered right as it begins to blett, so watch the crop closely near harvest.

directions: Plant dormant, grafted trees in early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. A popular traditional English perry pear valued for producing consistently excellent, low-tannin, medium-acid perry, it bears small, fiddly fruit that yields an extremely sweet, sharp, fruity, and intense juice when milled at just the right moment of ripeness. Its low-tannin profile makes it a favorite for blending into lighter, more approachable perries, in contrast to the harsh bittersharp varieties that need long aging to soften. Harvest the fruit once it begins to drop and blett in early fall, then mill and press promptly for perry.

planting.note: Plant dormant, grafted trees in early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Moorcroft grows into an extremely tall tree with a narrow ripening window, so plan for a tall ladder or long-handled picking tools at harvest.

directions: Plant dormant, grafted trees in early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. Classified among the bitter, high-tannin, low-acid perry pears, it can be difficult to work with thanks to its narrow ripening window and the sheer height of its trees, but the resulting juice is prized by perry makers, with well-bletted fruit described as tasting somewhere between fresh dates and a bakewell tart with custard. Its high tannin content gives finished perry real structure and aging potential, making it a valued component of traditional Three Counties perry blends. Harvest the hard fruit once it begins dropping in fall, let it sweat and blett for several days, then mill and press for perry.
sources: Slow Food USA — Ark of Taste

planting.note: Plant dormant, grafted trees in early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Merrylegs is a traditional English perry pear grown solely for pressing rather than fresh eating.

directions: Plant dormant, grafted trees in early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. One of a number of old West Country perry pears whimsically named for the reputed effects of their potent drink, it is classified as a sweet type with low tannin and low acid, yielding an easy-drinking, mellow perry with less of the harsh astringency typical of the bittersharp varieties. Like other true perry pears it bears hard, astringent fruit of no value for fresh eating, grown purely for fermenting into traditional English perry. Harvest the hard fruit once it begins dropping in early fall, let it sweat for a few days to soften, then mill and press for perry.

planting.note: Plant dormant, grafted trees in early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Judge Amphlett fruit can turn unpleasant if left to blett too far, so perry makers must judge the moment of pressing carefully.

directions: Plant dormant, grafted trees in early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. Named for the Assizes court judge Richard Amphlett, one of several traditional Three Counties perry pears commemorating individuals, it is a medium sharp type with medium acidity and low tannin. Its bletted fruit is notoriously unpredictable, developing into either a rich, sweet, delicious pear or, if left too long, an antiseptic, unpleasant one, making it one of the trickier traditional perry pears to work with despite its good potential quality. Harvest the hard fruit once it begins dropping in early fall, monitor bletting closely, and mill and press for perry as soon as the fruit reaches its best condition.
sources: Slow Food USA — Ark of Taste

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Ekmek is self-fertile but yields more heavily with a second quince variety nearby for cross-pollination.

directions: Plant bare-root or container trees in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. A Turkish cultivar whose name means "bread" in Turkish, it bears large, golden, slightly fuzzy, intensely fragrant fruit with crisp flesh that carries enough natural sugar to be eaten fresh off the tree, unlike most quince, though it is more commonly gently roasted or poached, or processed into jam, candy, compote, or custard. Brought to the United States from Turkey in 1986 and released from USDA quarantine in 1991, it has since been highly rated by American pomologists for its flavor and disease resistance. The tree is productive and hardy, blooming with pale pink spring flowers before fruit ripens in fall. Harvest in fall once fragrant and fully colored, and use fresh or in cooked preparations.

common_name: Cydora Robusta Quince (Disease-Resistant European Fruiting and Rootstock Selection)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Cydora Robusta is self-fertile, slow-growing, and notably tolerant of fire blight and mildew compared to many other quince selections.

directions: Plant bare-root or container trees in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. A German-bred selection valued for its climatic robustness, it shows good tolerance of fire blight and resistance to mildew and leaf spot disease, with fruit that resists the internal browning that troubles some other quince cultivars. It bears large, pear-shaped, bright yellow, slightly hairy fruit with medium-firm, creamy yellow pulp and an intense quince aroma, produced in heavy crops in October on a hardy, upright, slow-growing tree well suited to smaller gardens. Its fragrant pink spring blossom attracts pollinators even though the tree needs none for fruit set. Harvest in October once golden and fragrant, and use for jams, jellies, pastes, and compotes.

planting.note: Plant bare-root rootstock liners in late winter while dormant in well-drained soil in full sun, then graft a compatible desired pear variety onto the young rootstock, using an interstem for varieties incompatible with quince; Provence is a dwarfing understock, not grown for its own fruit.

directions: Plant bare-root rootstock liners in late winter while dormant in well-drained soil in full sun, then graft a compatible desired pear variety onto the young rootstock, using an interstem for varieties incompatible with quince. A long-used traditional French quince selection, it has historically served as a dwarfing rootstock for pear, producing a tree slightly larger than the more common Quince A or Quince C rootstocks while still offering good precocity and size control compared to seedling pear rootstocks. As with other quince rootstocks, many pear varieties are graft-incompatible with it, so an interstem of a compatible pear variety is often bench-grafted between the Provence rootstock and the desired scion. It is hardy to about -10°F, suiting it to zones 6 through 8. Graft or double-work a desired named pear variety onto young rootstock in late winter, and reserve it for growers wanting a somewhat larger tree than Quince A or BA29 provide.
